title: The Second Attempt at Riverside Theatre
author: ONE HOME original short-reader collection
pages: Maya arrived at Riverside Theatre before the afternoon activity began. The room was quiet, but there was plenty to prepare. On a small table lay a ruler, ready to be used. Then the organiser explained the difficulty: the first design kept falling over. Maya had expected a simple afternoon and felt uncertain. Instead of pretending to know the answer, Maya asked for a few minutes to look carefully. There was still time to understand what had happened before anyone made a decision.

The first step was to test one change at a time on a small model. This took longer than making a quick guess, but it gave the group something useful to work with. Maya wrote down what was known and put a question mark beside what still needed checking. A friend suggested rushing ahead. “If we get the first part wrong, we may have to do everything twice,” Maya replied. Together they compared the information. One detail mattered more than the others: a plan had to work for the people who would actually use it.

Soon the group had a possible answer. They could widen the base and test the design again. Maya explained the idea, then asked the others what might go wrong. At first, nobody spoke. After a moment, a younger visitor raised a concern. The group listened rather than dismissing it. They changed a small part of the plan and tried it on a limited scale. The trial was not perfect, but it showed them what to improve. Maya used a ruler to keep track of the next step.

When the visitors arrived, the group put the revised plan into practice. Someone who had missed the discussion asked why they had chosen this approach. Maya explained both the problem and the reason for the decision. That explanation helped the newcomer take part without feeling left behind. During the afternoon, the team checked how things were going. They did not assume that silence meant success. They asked people directly and made another small adjustment when it was needed.

By the end of the afternoon, Riverside Theatre felt different. The original problem had become a chance to practise being patient. Maya returned a ruler to the table and wrote a note for the next group: “Check, listen, try, then improve.” The organiser thanked everyone, including the visitor whose question had changed the plan. Maya was pleased, but the best part was knowing how the group had reached its answer. They had not needed one person to know everything. They had needed people who were willing to think together.

questions.prompt: What difficulty did the group face?
choices: new visitors found the entrance difficult to locate
two posters gave different opening times
two groups wanted to use the same space
the first design kept falling over
questions.hint: Look back at what the group actually did.

questions.prompt: What did the group decide to do?
choices: widen the base and test the design again
replace the old poster with a clear new notice
agree a timetable that gave each group a turn
add simple signs at the confusing turning points
questions.hint: Look back at what the group actually did.

questions.prompt: Why did the group test a small version first?
choices: To discover problems before using the full plan
To make the task last forever
questions.hint: Think about what the trial revealed.
